title: Git & Version Control
description: Track changes and collaborate effectively with Git. Master branching, merging, rebasing, and professional team workflows.

topics.title: Git Basics
topics.content:
### What is Git?

Git is a **distributed version control system**. Every developer has a complete copy of the repository — including its full history — on their local machine. This is different from centralized systems (like SVN) where there's one central server.

#### Core Concepts

| Concept | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Repository (repo)** | A directory tracked by Git, containing all project files and history. |
| **Working tree** | The files you see and edit on disk. |
| **Staging area (index)** | A preparation zone where you build up a commit. |
| **Commit** | A permanent snapshot of staged changes, stored with a SHA-1 hash. |
| **HEAD** | A pointer to the current commit (usually the tip of the current branch). |

#### Essential Commands

```bash
# Initialize a new repository
git init

# Clone an existing repository
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

# Check the status of your working tree
git status

# See what changed (unstaged)
git diff

# See what is staged
git diff --staged

# View commit history
git log --oneline --graph --decorate
```

---

topics.title: Commits: Staging and Saving
topics.content:
### The Three-Stage Workflow

Git's staging area is what separates it from most other VCS tools. It lets you craft precise, logical commits even when your working tree has unrelated changes.

```bash
# Stage a specific file
git add src/api/auth.ts

# Stage parts of a file (interactive patch)
git add -p src/api/auth.ts

# Stage all changes in the current directory
git add .

# Commit staged changes
git commit -m "feat(auth): add JWT refresh token rotation"

# Stage and commit tracked files in one step
git commit -am "fix: handle null user in profile route"

# Amend the most recent commit (before pushing)
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

#### Writing Good Commit Messages

Follow the **Conventional Commits** specification:

```
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

[optional body]

[optional footer]
```

Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`

**Good**: `feat(auth): add OAuth2 Google login`  
**Bad**: `fixed stuff`, `wip`, `asdfgh`

topics.title: Branching
topics.content:
### Branches are Cheap

A branch in Git is just a lightweight pointer to a commit. Creating a branch costs nothing — it's a 41-byte file. Use branches liberally.

```bash
# List all branches
git branch -a

# Create a new branch
git branch feature/user-auth

# Create and switch in one command
git checkout -b feature/user-auth
# Modern equivalent:
git switch -c feature/user-auth

# Switch to an existing branch
git switch main

# Delete a branch (after merging)
git branch -d feature/user-auth

# Force delete (unmerged changes)
git branch -D feature/user-auth

# Push a branch to remote
git push -u origin feature/user-auth
```

#### Branch Naming Conventions

```
feature/add-payment-gateway
bugfix/login-redirect-loop
hotfix/critical-sql-injection
release/v2.1.0
chore/upgrade-dependencies
```

topics.title: Merging vs Rebasing
topics.content:
### Two Ways to Integrate Changes

#### Merge: Preserves History

Merge creates a new "merge commit" that joins two branches. The history shows exactly when branches diverged and rejoined.

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature/user-auth

# Fast-forward merge (if no divergence)
git merge --ff-only feature/user-auth

# Always create a merge commit (no fast-forward)
git merge --no-ff feature/user-auth
```

#### Rebase: Linear History

Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch. The result is a clean, linear history — but it rewrites commit SHAs.

```bash
# Rebase feature branch onto main
git switch feature/user-auth
git rebase main

# Interactive rebase: squash, reorder, edit commits
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```

#### The Golden Rule of Rebasing

> **Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote branch.**

Rebasing rewrites history. If others have based work on those commits, they will have a bad time.

| | Merge | Rebase |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **History** | Preserves all branches | Linear, clean |
| **Safety** | Always safe | Unsafe on shared branches |
| **Use case** | Integrating finished features | Cleaning up local commits |

topics.title: Conflict Resolution
topics.content:
### When Two Branches Change the Same Lines

A merge conflict occurs when Git can't automatically reconcile two versions of the same file.

```bash
# After a conflicted merge, Git marks the conflicted files
git status
# Both modified:   src/auth/login.ts

# Open the file — you'll see conflict markers:
```

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
const timeout = 3600;  // your change
=======
const timeout = 7200;  // their change
>>>>>>> feature/extend-session
```

```bash
# After manually resolving, stage the file
git add src/auth/login.ts

# Complete the merge
git commit

# Or abort and go back to before the merge
git merge --abort
```

#### Pro Tip: Use a Merge Tool

```bash
# Use VS Code as the merge tool
git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait $MERGED'
git mergetool
```

topics.title: Git Workflows
topics.content:
### How Teams Organize Their Branches

#### GitHub Flow (Simple, Recommended)

Perfect for teams deploying continuously:

1. `main` is always deployable.
2. Create a branch for every feature/fix.
3. Open a Pull Request when ready.
4. Merge to `main` after review.
5. Deploy immediately.

#### Git Flow (Complex, for Scheduled Releases)

Uses two permanent branches (`main`, `develop`) and three supporting types (`feature/`, `release/`, `hotfix/`).

#### Trunk-Based Development

Everyone commits to `main` (or `trunk`) multiple times per day. Feature flags hide incomplete work. Requires strong CI.

#### Which to Use?

| Team Size | Release Cadence | Recommended Workflow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1–5 devs | Continuous | GitHub Flow |
| 5–20 devs | Scheduled | Git Flow |
| 20+ devs | Continuous | Trunk-Based |

topics.title: Semantic Versioning
topics.content:
### Version Numbers That Mean Something

**SemVer** format: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

```
v2.4.1
^  ^  ^
|  |  └── PATCH: backwards-compatible bug fixes
|  └───── MINOR: new backwards-compatible features
└──────── MAJOR: breaking changes
```

#### Examples

```bash
# Bug fix (no API changes)
v1.0.0 → v1.0.1

# New feature (old code still works)
v1.0.1 → v1.1.0

# Breaking change (old code may break)
v1.1.0 → v2.0.0
```

#### Pre-release Labels

```
v2.0.0-alpha.1    # Early testing
v2.0.0-beta.3     # Feature complete, bug fixes only
v2.0.0-rc.1       # Release candidate
v2.0.0            # Stable release
```

#### Git Tags

```bash
# Create an annotated tag
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release v1.2.0: add payment module"

# Push tags to remote
git push origin --tags

# List all tags
git tag -l
```
